                                    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS


                               Request for Public Hearing
 Project No. 58481 — Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA
                                          §37.0561

  Filed by: Zack Butler / EnerShield AI          April 12, 2026                     16 TAC §22.103



Pursuant to 16 TAC §22.103 and the Commission's standing procedures for public participation in
rulemaking proceedings, EnerShield AI respectfully requests that the Commission set this matter for a public
hearing.


BASIS FOR THE REQUEST

EnerShield AI has filed in this docket empirical research constituting the first fleet-scale satellite-based
measurement of passive infrastructure degradation across the Texas data center sector. The research —
The Invisible Tax: Quantifying the Energy, Water, and Grid Impacts of Cool Roof Degradation Across the
Texas Data Center Fleet (April 2026, Exhibit A to our supplemental comments filed concurrently herewith) —
presents nine years of spectral data from 425 facilities representing 27.0 million square feet of Texas data
center roof area.

The findings are empirical, bounded, and directly relevant to the Commission's rulemaking objectives under
PURA §37.0561. Specifically, they establish that existing large load facilities impose an estimated 47.4 MW
of avoidable coincident peak demand on the ERCOT grid during summer scarcity events — demand
attributable to the degradation of passive building infrastructure that could be eliminated through low-cost
maintenance interventions with ROI exceeding 1,000%.

The full implications of these findings for the proposed rule — including the appropriate scope of passive
efficiency disclosure requirements, the design of positive incentive structures, and the technical standards for
satellite-based monitoring — present complex factual and technical questions that would benefit significantly
from evidentiary hearing and direct examination by Commission Staff and other parties.

A public hearing would provide an opportunity for EnerShield AI to present testimony on the research
methodology, respond to technical questions, and assist the Commission in developing a durable,
evidence-based regulatory record on passive infrastructure performance as a component of large load
interconnection standards.


UNIQUE CONTRIBUTION TO THE RECORD

Every other party filing comments in this proceeding is addressing the future demand coming in through the
interconnection queue — queue management, financial security levels, study fees, and site control
requirements. EnerShield AI is the only party in this proceeding that has placed on record a quantified
measurement of the avoidable demand already operating on the ERCOT grid.

That distinction is important. The Commission is simultaneously being asked to (1) manage the costs of new
large load interconnection and (2) maintain ERCOT grid reliability during summer peak events. EnerShield
AI's research addresses both objectives with a single, unified dataset: the same 47.4 MW of avoidable
  demand that stresses the grid on peak summer afternoons is also the same demand that could be eliminated
 — not curtailed, not shifted, but permanently eliminated — through a maintenance program that costs a
 fraction of a single hour of ERCOT scarcity pricing.


 OFFER OF TESTIMONY

 EnerShield AI is prepared to present direct testimony from Zack Butler regarding:

     (1) The satellite-based spectral methodology used to measure fleet-wide cool roof degradation across
     425 Texas data center facilities using nine years of Sentinel-2 imagery;

     (2) The physical and economic mechanisms linking albedo degradation to coincident peak demand on
     the ERCOT grid, including the thermal lag that synchronizes the albedo penalty with afternoon scarcity
     events;

     (3) The structural split-incentive problem that produces systematic underinvestment in passive
     infrastructure maintenance, and why voluntary market forces alone will not correct it; and
     (4) The proposed regulatory framework for integrating passive efficiency monitoring into large load
     interconnection standards, including the technical specifications for a PUCT-recognized third-party
     spectral monitoring program.

 Mr. Butler is available at the Commission's convenience and will make himself available for any pre-hearing
 technical conference or Staff consultation that would assist the Commission's analysis. His background — a
 decade as a hands-on commercial roofing contractor combined with a prior career as an energy commodity
 trader at ExxonMobil, Phillips 66, BP, and Amazon — is unusual in this proceeding and uniquely relevant to
 the intersection of building envelope physics and ERCOT marginal pricing that this research addresses.


 PRAYER FOR RELIEF

  EnerShield AI respectfully requests that the Commission:
     (1) Set this matter for a public hearing pursuant to 16 TAC §22.103;
     (2) Designate EnerShield AI as a party with standing to present testimony and respond to Commission
     Staff questions in this proceeding;
     (3) Accept the full research paper, The Invisible Tax (April 2026), as evidentiary record in this
     proceeding; and
     (4) Consider the recommendations set forth in the concurrently filed Supplemental Comments in
     developing the final rule under 16 TAC §25.194.

STATEMENT OF INTEREST
EnerShield AI submits these supplemental comments to transmit updated empirical research directly
relevant to the Commission's consideration of large load interconnection standards under proposed 16 TAC
§25.194, and to formally request a public hearing on this matter. These comments supersede our initial filing
(Item No. 136, filed April 10, 2026) and attach the full research paper, The Invisible Tax: Quantifying the
Energy, Water, and Grid Impacts of Cool Roof Degradation Across the Texas Data Center Fleet (April 2026),
as Exhibit A.


ABOUT THE COMMENTER

Zack Butler is the co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer of Blind Mice Labs and its EnerShield AI platform.
He is not a licensed engineer — and that is precisely what makes this research credible.

He has personally inspected, bid, and managed commercial roof systems across hundreds of facilities in the
Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston markets. He knows what a degraded TPO membrane looks like from 20 feet
away, what it costs to fix, and what happens when an operator ignores it for a decade. That ground-level
knowledge is what drove him to look for the same patterns from satellite altitude.

Before entering the roofing industry, Mr. Butler spent a decade in energy commodity trading and enterprise
risk management at ExxonMobil, Phillips 66, BP, and Amazon. He understands ERCOT marginal pricing,
scarcity events, and the economics of coincident peak demand in the same way most facility managers
understand their utility bills — intuitively and precisely. He holds a B.S. in Economics (Cum Laude) from
Texas A&M; University and an MBA from the SMU Cox School of Business, and is a veteran of the United
States Navy. He is an active member of NAIOP Houston, where he is the only commercial roofing
professional in the chapter.

The intersection of those two backgrounds — rooftop practitioner and energy markets quantitative analyst —
is what produced this research. It did not come from a laboratory. It came from recognizing that the same
membrane degradation patterns visible on every commercial rooftop in Texas are also visible in nine years of
Sentinel-2 satellite data, and that the financial and grid consequences of that degradation had never been
measured at fleet scale. Now they have been.


THE PROBLEM: AN EXISTING, UNREGULATED LOAD ALREADY ON THE GRID
 The Commission's proposed rule under 16 TAC §25.194 appropriately addresses the future interconnection
of new large loads. EnerShield AI urges the Commission to simultaneously recognize an existing burden that
current rulemaking has not addressed: the avoidable coincident peak demand imposed on the ERCOT grid
every summer afternoon by the degraded passive infrastructure of data centers already operating in Texas.

EnerShield AI conducted the first fleet-scale empirical analysis of cool roof degradation across the Texas
data center sector, analyzing nine years (2017–2025) of Sentinel-2 satellite multispectral imagery across 425
facilities representing 27.0 million square feet of roof area. The findings establish a systemic and measurable
failure:

    • The fleet-wide average solar reflectance has degraded to 0.365 — well below the Cool Roof Rating
    Council (CRRC) minimum of 0.55.
    • 95.3% of analyzed facilities are operating below the CRRC minimum standard.
    • 31.4% of facilities are in a "Critical" risk tier, indicating severe degradation with high probability of
    moisture infiltration and structural damage.

This demand is not hypothetical, and it is not uniformly distributed across the day. It peaks at approximately
4:00 PM on hot summer afternoons — precisely when ERCOT scarcity events occur — due to the thermal
lag between peak solar irradiance and peak HVAC response. At the $5,000/MWh scarcity cap, 47.4 MW of
avoidable demand costs the grid over $237,000 per scarcity hour, costs socialized across all Texas
ratepayers.


THE INCENTIVE GAP

This is not operator negligence. It is a structural failure with a predictable cause. The industry operates under
a "build and forget" paradigm for passive infrastructure. Developers invest in high-albedo membranes at
construction to satisfy LEED standards or local codes, but there is no regulatory or financial mechanism
requiring ongoing performance monitoring after commissioning.

The colocation business model compounds this with a classic split-incentive problem: the facility operator
owns the building envelope and bears the cost of roof maintenance, while the tenant pays the utility bills and
captures 100% of the energy savings from a clean, reflective roof. No individual party is acting irrationally —
there is simply no mechanism aligning the cost of maintenance with the value of the energy and water saved.
The result is systematic underinvestment, and 47.4 MW of avoidable coincident peak demand on the
ERCOT grid every summer afternoon.


RECOMMENDED FRAMEWORK: CONNECT PASSIVE EFFICIENCY TO
INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
 The Commission has an opportunity to close this incentive gap directly within the 16 TAC §25.194
framework. EnerShield AI recommends the Commission consider the following additions:

    1. Passive Efficiency Disclosure as a Condition of Interconnection.

    Large load customers seeking new interconnection or capacity expansion should be required to disclose
    the current solar reflectance performance of their existing building envelope as part of the site
    information package. Satellite-based spectral assessment is now mature, cost-effective, and available at
    scale.

    2. Preferred Interconnection Status for Verified Passive Efficiency.

    Facilities that demonstrate and maintain verified roof albedo at or above the CRRC minimum of 0.55 —
    confirmed through a PUCT-recognized third-party spectral monitoring program — should receive
    favorable treatment in interconnection queue prioritization. Facilities whose degraded passive
    infrastructure adds avoidable coincident peak demand should bear those costs rather than socializing
    them to all Texas ratepayers.

    3. Maintenance Escrow Requirements at Permitting.

    Require new large load developers to establish escrow accounts at permitting, funded to cover periodic
    roof cleaning and eventual membrane replacement. This directly addresses the split-incentive problem
    in colocation models by ensuring maintenance funds exist regardless of changes in ownership or
    tenancy.

    4. Cross-Reference to Project 58482.

    The voluntary demand reduction program being developed in Project 58482 should explicitly recognize
    verified roof restoration as an eligible demand reduction measure. For the average Texas data center in
    this cohort, a professional roof cleaning costing $2,500–$7,500 eliminates an estimated $58,937 in
    annual excess cooling costs and reduces coincident peak demand by 100–300 kW — an ROI exceeding
    1,000% with payback measured in weeks.



CONCLUSION

The Commission is building a framework for the future of large load integration in Texas. That framework will
be incomplete if it addresses only the demand coming in through the interconnection queue while ignoring
the avoidable demand already running on the grid. The two problems have the same solution: align operator
incentives with grid reliability outcomes through monitoring, transparency, and positive incentives for
proactive performance.

EnerShield AI stands ready to provide fleet-level spectral data, technical consultation, and testimony to
support the Commission's analysis. The full research paper is attached as Exhibit A.

The Invisible Tax: Quantifying the Energy, Water, and Grid
Impacts of Cool Roof Degradation Across the Texas Data
Center Fleet
Research Paper | April 2026

Abstract
The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure in Texas, driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud computing demands, has
placed unprecedented strain on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid and local water resources. While new facility
designs increasingly incorporate advanced liquid cooling and high-efficiency IT equipment, the ongoing operational performance
of the building envelope—specifically the thermal reflectance of “cool roof” membranes—remains largely unmonitored and
unregulated. This study presents the first fleet-scale empirical analysis of cool roof degradation across the data center sector,
using nine years (2017–2025) of Sentinel-2 satellite multispectral imagery to analyze the broadband albedo (solar reflectance) of
425 data center facilities across Texas, representing 27.0 million square feet of total portfolio roof area. The findings reveal a
systemic failure of passive cooling infrastructure: the fleet-wide average albedo has degraded to a 2024 measured value of 0.365
across 191 facilities with complete spectral data, with 95.3% of analyzed facilities operating below the Cool Roof Rating Council
(CRRC) minimum threshold of 0.55. This degradation imposes an “invisible tax” on facility operations, generating an estimated
$11.26 million in excess annual cooling energy costs for the 191 measured facilities in 2024—scaling to an estimated $20.6
million annually across the full 425-facility Texas portfolio when extrapolated by verified roof area. The measured cohort also
wastes an additional 25.1 million gallons of cooling tower water per year (46.0 million gallons fleet-wide). Furthermore, this
localized inefficiency scales to a systemic grid vulnerability, adding an estimated 25.9 MW of coincident peak demand during
ERCOT summer scarcity events (47.4 MW fleet-wide when extrapolated by verified roof area). The results demonstrate that passive
envelope degradation is a material, unpriced operational risk, and that continuous spectral monitoring combined with proactive
membrane restoration represents one of the highest-ROI sustainability interventions available to data center operators today.
Keywords: cool roof degradation, data center sustainability, solar reflectance, Sentinel-2, ERCOT, water efficiency, building
envelope, Texas, remote sensing

1. Introduction
1.1. The Texas Data Center Boom and Its Resource Demands
The proliferation of data centers in Texas represents one of the most consequential industrial expansions in the state’s modern
history. Driven by a favorable regulatory environment, relatively low energy costs, land availability, and the explosive growth of
generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large-scale cloud computing, Texas has emerged as a global hub for hyperscale and
colocation facilities [1]. The Texas Real Estate Research Center at Texas A&M University documented this transformation in a 2025
report noting that the state is poised to host more AI data centers than anywhere else in the world, with hundreds of billions of
dollars in committed capital flowing into the sector [1].
This growth has introduced profound and escalating challenges regarding resource consumption. Data centers are among the
most energy-intensive building typologies in existence, and their cooling systems—which must continuously remove the waste
heat generated by servers and networking equipment—are the primary consumers of both electricity and water. The Electric
Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages the grid serving approximately 90% of the state’s electric load, has identified
data center growth as one of the most significant drivers of peak demand uncertainty over the next decade. Simultaneously, Texas
faces a chronic and worsening water deficit, with the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) documenting a current 4.8-million-
acre-foot annual shortage that data center expansion threatens to deepen [13].
 The industry’s response to these pressures has been almost exclusively focused on the active components of data center cooling:
transitioning from traditional air-cooled systems to direct-to-chip liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers, and immersion
cooling technologies. These innovations have driven meaningful improvements in Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Water
Usage Effectiveness (WUE). However, this focus on active systems has created a significant blind spot: the passive thermal
performance of the building envelope.
1.2. The Role of the Building Envelope
A data center’s roof is the primary thermal interface between the facility and the external environment. In Texas, where summer
solar irradiance regularly exceeds 1,000 W/m² and ambient temperatures can reach 40°C (104°F), the roof’s ability to reflect solar
radiation directly dictates the magnitude of conductive heat gain that must be removed by the cooling system. A roof with high
solar reflectance (albedo) absorbs minimal solar energy and re-emits much of what it does absorb as longwave radiation, keeping
the roof surface cool and minimizing heat transfer into the building. Conversely, a dark or degraded roof can reach surface
temperatures exceeding 70°C (158°F), driving substantial heat gain into the facility’s plenum, CRAC units, and ultimately the IT
load.
To mitigate this, modern data centers are almost universally constructed with “cool roofs”—highly reflective white membranes,
typically Thermoplastic Polyolefin (TPO) or Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC), designed to maintain an initial solar reflectance of 0.65–0.80
and a minimum aged reflectance of 0.55 per the Cool Roof Rating Council (CRRC) standard [14]. These membranes represent a
significant capital investment and, when properly maintained, provide a passive cooling benefit that reduces cooling energy
consumption by an estimated 10–30% compared to a conventional dark roof.
As a comprehensive 2024 review of data center cooling strategies concluded, “the feasibility and effect of designing walls, roofs,
and windows in a building envelope for cooling DCs are key research areas for future work because they have been identified as
the most effective passive strategies but have not yet been investigated in the study of DCs” [2]. This paper directly addresses that
identified gap.
1.3. Cool Roof Degradation: A Known but Unquantified Problem
Cool roofs are not static assets. Environmental exposure, ultraviolet radiation, particulate accumulation (including industrial soot,
pollen, and biological growth such as algae and lichen), and membrane weathering cause solar reflectance to degrade over time.
The rate of degradation depends on the membrane material, the local climate, and the proximity of the facility to pollution
sources.
A landmark 2025 study by Bonanni et al. analyzed 18,565 census blocks in New York City with cool roofs installed between 2014
and 2020 and found that 24.56% experienced significant reflectance degradation within six years [3]. The study noted that the
largest proportion of degradation (57.39%) occurred within the first two years of installation, and concluded that “municipal
maintenance initiatives are needed to ensure the urban heat mitigation potential of cool roofs is sustained.” While this study
focused on residential and commercial buildings, its findings have direct implications for the data center sector, where the
thermal consequences of degradation are amplified by the continuous, high-density heat loads generated by IT equipment.
Despite this evidence, the extent and operational impact of cool roof degradation across the data center industry have never been
empirically quantified at fleet scale. Individual facility managers may observe visible soiling on their roofs, but without systematic
measurement, the financial and environmental penalty remains invisible—a tax that is paid every month on the utility bill without
ever being itemized.
1.4. Research Objectives
This study addresses the following research questions:
   1. What is the current state of cool roof reflectance across the Texas data center fleet, and how has it changed from 2017 to
      2025?
   2. What is the quantifiable financial penalty (excess energy cost) attributable to albedo degradation?
   3. What is the corresponding water consumption penalty, specifically the excess cooling tower water use driven by increased
      thermal loads?
   4. How does the aggregate excess demand from degraded data center roofs affect the ERCOT grid, particularly during peak
      summer scarcity events?
    5. What are the disparities in performance across different operators, and what do they reveal about industry maintenance
      practices?

2. Methodology
2.1. Facility Identification and Bounding
The study analyzed 425 data center facilities located within the state of Texas. Facility locations and roof polygons were sourced
from a proprietary database cross-referenced with public records and satellite imagery. To ensure the integrity of the spectral
extraction, exact roof polygons were used rather than bounding boxes, eliminating contamination from surrounding parking lots,
vegetation, or adjacent structures. Of the 425 facilities, 403 had sufficient cloud-free satellite imagery to be included in the
longitudinal analysis, and 191 had complete data for the 2024 focal year.
2.2. Remote Sensing and Spectral Extraction
Albedo (solar reflectance) and related spectral indices were extracted using Sentinel-2 Level-2A (L2A) imagery via the Sentinel Hub
Statistical API. The L2A product provides atmospherically corrected surface reflectance, which is critical for accurate longitudinal
comparison.
Exact Polygon Masking and Pixel Sampling: To ensure the integrity of the spectral extraction, exact roof polygons (stored as
GeoJSON in the dc_facilities database) were used as the bounding geometry for the Sentinel Hub API requests. This method
( sentinel2_polygon_v2 ) strictly clips the Sentinel-2 raster to the building footprint, eliminating contamination from surrounding
parking lots, vegetation, or adjacent structures.
Sentinel-2 provides multispectral imagery at varying spatial resolutions: 10 meters for visible and near-infrared bands (B04, B08)
and 20 meters for shortwave infrared bands (B11). At 10-meter resolution, each pixel represents 100 square meters, yielding
approximately 50 pure roof pixels for a typical 5,000 m² data center roof. At 20-meter resolution, each pixel represents 400 square
meters, yielding approximately 12 pixels for the same roof. The Statistical API aggregates these pixels, returning the mean and
standard deviation for each spectral band across the polygon.
Cloud Masking and Temporal Aggregation: Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance products have a stated absolute radiometric
uncertainty of approximately 5% (or 0.02 to 0.05 reflectance units) depending on atmospheric conditions [8]. To mitigate this
uncertainty and ensure high data quality:
    1. Strict Cloud Masking: A custom Evalscript was used to apply the Scene Classification Layer (SCL). Only pixels classified as
       vegetation (4), bare soil (5), water (6), or unclassified (7) were considered valid. Pixels classified as cloud (medium or high
       probability, 8-9), thin cirrus (10), or snow (11) were strictly excluded from the statistical aggregation.
    2. Temporal Aggregation: We extracted all available scenes during the summer months (June–August) for each year (2017–
       2025). The API was configured to accept scenes with up to 50% overall cloud coverage (relaxed to 80% if necessary), relying
       on the pixel-level SCL mask to filter out the clouds over the specific roof polygon.
    3. Seasonal Means: The daily valid pixel statistics were then averaged across the entire summer season. Averaging across 15–
       25 valid scene-days per facility-year significantly reduces random atmospheric noise and bidirectional reflectance
       distribution function (BRDF) effects.
Broadband albedo was calculated using the Liang (2001) narrow-to-broadband conversion formula adapted for Sentinel-2 bands:
Albedo = 0.356 * B04 + 0.130 * B08 + 0.373 * B11 + 0.085



2.3. Baseline Establishment
A critical methodological requirement is distinguishing between manufacturer initial reflectance (0.65–0.80), the Cool Roof Rating
Council (CRRC) minimum qualifying reflectance (0.55), and the observed fleet baseline (0.372). These figures describe different
points in a roof’s lifecycle. Manufacturer initial reflectance is the performance of a new membrane before weathering. The CRRC
minimum is the performance floor for new products. The observed fleet baseline (0.372) is the measured summer-season albedo
as observed by Sentinel-2 in 2017.
 By 2017, the majority of these roofs had been in service for 5–15 years. The gap between the CRRC minimum (0.55) and the
observed 2017 baseline (0.372) represents approximately 0.18 albedo units of degradation that had already occurred before the
study measurement window begins. The observed baseline therefore already includes significant pre-2017 degradation.
Consequently, the $11.26 million annual energy penalty quantified here represents only the degradation that occurred during the
2017–2024 measurement window. The total lifetime energy penalty is substantially larger. Under realistic conditions, this
methodology inherently underestimates true degradation and its associated financial impact.
Membrane type assignments were initially derived from construction records and operator-reported data, then field-verified via
high-resolution Google Earth satellite imagery review for a representative sample of facilities. This verification process corrected
several initial assignments: five facilities previously classified as EPDM were re-classified as TPO/PVC (2), Modified Bitumen (2),
and Unknown (1); and one facility previously classified as TPO was re-classified as Modified Bitumen based on visible surface
texture and color characteristics. The corrected fleet composition is: TPO (394 facilities, 92.7%), Modified Bitumen (19 facilities,
4.5%), Unknown (6 facilities, 1.4%), BUR (5 facilities, 1.2%), and Metal (1 facility, 0.2%). The fleet is dominated by TPO membranes,
which have a well-documented initial reflectance of 0.70–0.80 and a CRRC-certified 3-year aged reflectance of 0.55–0.65. The
larger-than-expected Modified Bitumen count (4.5%) reflects the prevalence of older stock in the Houston and Fort Worth
markets, where BUR and Mod Bit were the standard commercial roofing specification prior to the widespread adoption of TPO in
the early 2000s. Notably, all facilities initially classified as EPDM were found to be either TPO, Modified Bitumen, BUR, Metal, or
bad addresses (Unknown), confirming that EPDM is exceptionally rare in the Texas data center market. The model accounts for
this through membrane-type-specific calibration coefficients, ensuring that the analysis isolates incremental performance loss
within the observation window rather than total lifecycle degradation.
2.4. Energy Impact Modeling
The excess cooling energy attributable to albedo degradation was calculated using a deterministic, physics-based model, which
was subsequently validated via Monte Carlo simulation to quantify uncertainty.
For each facility-year, the excess heat gain (ΔQ, in kWh/year) was calculated as: ΔQ = (α_baseline - α_current) * I_annual *
A_roof * η_envelope

Where:
      α_baseline     is the baseline albedo.
        α_current is the measured current albedo.

        I_annual is the annual solar irradiance at the facility location (kWh/m²/year, sourced from the Google Solar API).

        A_roof is the verified roof area (m²).

        η_envelope is an envelope efficiency factor (0.85) accounting for the fraction of roof heat gain that actually reaches the
       conditioned space, acknowledging that roofs are insulated.
This excess heat gain was converted to excess cooling energy (kWh/year) by dividing by an assumed cooling system Coefficient of
Performance (COP) of 3.5. While modern hyperscale facilities may achieve higher COPs (e.g., 4.5–5.0), the Texas fleet includes a
vast number of legacy enterprise and colocation facilities where COPs of 2.5–3.0 are common. A fleet-wide average of 3.5
represents a defensible middle ground. The resulting excess cooling energy was multiplied by a flat commercial electricity rate
($0.065/kWh) to yield the annual financial penalty. This flat rate is highly conservative, as it ignores demand charges and
coincident peak pricing, which disproportionately affect data centers during hot summer afternoons when albedo penalties are
highest.
It is critical to note that real-world commercial electricity pricing is rarely flat; it typically includes substantial demand charges
(often $10–$20 per kW), time-of-use (TOU) peak pricing premiums, and exposure to wholesale scarcity pricing during grid
emergencies. Because the albedo penalty peaks during hot summer afternoons when these demand charges and TOU rates are
highest, a flat $0.065/kWh rate significantly undervalues the true cost of the excess load. Because this incremental load is
concentrated during peak thermal conditions, it is disproportionately exposed to demand charges, time-of-use pricing, and
scarcity pricing events. The use of a flat rate therefore understates real-world cost exposure, and the modeled financial impact
should be interpreted as a conservative lower bound.
 2.4.1. Physical Basis for Albedo-Driven Cooling Load
The causal link between roof albedo and data center cooling load is governed by fundamental thermodynamics. The solar heat
gain through a roof is directly proportional to solar absorptance (1 − α), where α is the albedo. When albedo decreases due to
membrane degradation, solar absorptance increases, driving higher roof surface temperatures and a larger conductive heat flux
into the building envelope. For a data center, this additional heat gain must be entirely removed by the HVAC system to maintain
strict IT inlet temperatures. The directional relationship is absolute: ↓ albedo → ↑ heat gain → ↑ cooling load. Empirical models
in hot climates indicate that for every 0.1 drop in albedo, annual cooling energy consumption increases by approximately 8.5–9.5
kWh per square meter of roof area [2][14]. This albedo-to-cooling-load relationship is approximately linear at first order, meaning
that even small incremental changes in albedo scale into material energy penalties when aggregated across fleet-level roof areas.
2.5. Water Waste Calculation
Water waste was calculated specifically for the evaporative cooling towers, as this represents the direct operational penalty of
increased cooling loads. Stormwater runoff was tracked separately but explicitly excluded from the waste totals.
The calculation utilizes the cooling_tower_water_coefficients reference table, which specifies the volume of water consumed
per kWh of cooling energy rejected. These coefficients vary by ASHRAE climate zone (Zone 2A for hot-humid Houston, Zone 3B for
hot-dry Dallas/Austin/San Antonio) and membrane type, derived from ASHRAE 189.1-2020 Table 6.4.3.1 [11], the EPA WaterSense
Cooling Tower Guide (2021) [12], and the Texas Water Development Board (2023) [13].
Crucially, the water consumption model was segmented by cooling system architecture. While large colocation and hyperscale
data centers utilize water-cooled chiller plants with evaporative cooling towers, smaller edge and enterprise facilities
predominantly utilize air-cooled packaged rooftop units (RTUs). Air-cooled RTUs consume zero water for heat rejection. However,
RTUs suffer a severe energy penalty when operating over a degraded, hot roof—laboratory tests demonstrate a 1.0% to 1.9%
increase in system power consumption per degree Celsius rise in condenser inlet air temperature [14].
To accurately segment the fleet, we developed a novel spectral classification algorithm using the Sentinel-2 Built-Up Roof Index
(BURI). Because a darkened, degraded membrane mimics the spectral signature of metal equipment, using current BURI values
conflates membrane degradation with actual mechanical equipment density. To eliminate this confound, the algorithm extracts
the BURI value at the facility’s peak albedo year (when the membrane was cleanest and its spectral contribution minimized). This
peak-year BURI provides a pure structural signal of mechanical equipment density. Facilities with a peak-year BURI ≥ 0.035 were
classified as RTU-dominant (zero water penalty), those < 0.025 as chiller-tower (full water penalty), and those between 0.025–
0.035 as mixed (partial water penalty), with secondary size-based heuristics applied. This spectral classification ensures that the
evaporative water penalty is applied only to the fraction of the fleet actually utilizing water-cooled chiller plants.
The classifier was validated against two ground-truth facilities: 1210 Integrity Drive (Richardson), which satellite imagery confirms
as RTU-dense (BURI_peak = 0.039), and 1000 Coit Road (Plano), which has a clean bare membrane (BURI_peak = 0.018). Applied
fleet-wide, the algorithm classified 131 of 191 facilities (68.6%) as RTU-dominant, 36 (18.8%) as chiller-tower, and 24 (12.6%) as
mixed. The resulting fleet-wide water waste figure of 7.88 million gallons/year is substantially lower than the naive assumption
that all facilities use cooling towers.

2.6. ERCOT Grid Impact Modeling
To quantify the impact on the Texas electrical grid, the annual excess cooling energy was translated into coincident peak demand
(MW). Because solar heat gain peaks during summer afternoons—exactly when the ERCOT grid experiences maximum stress—the
albedo penalty is highly coincident with grid peaks.
The peak demand impact was estimated by isolating the excess cooling load during the top 100 grid demand hours of the year. We
applied a conservative coincidence factor of 0.85, acknowledging thermal lag (the delay between peak solar irradiance and peak
HVAC load due to the building’s thermal mass).

3.8 The Compounding Effect: Insulation Thermal Derating and Moisture Degradation
While the primary mechanism of excess cooling load is the increased surface temperature of degraded membranes, this effect is
compounded by the temperature-dependent performance of the underlying insulation. Modern data center roofs are typically
insulated with polyisocyanurate (polyiso) rigid foam board, which provides high thermal resistance per inch. However, the R-value
of polyiso is not static; it is highly dependent on the mean temperature of the board.
Based on testing by the Building Science Corporation (BSC) and the National Roofing Contractors Association (NRCA), the thermal
resistance of polyiso peaks at moderate mean temperatures (between 36°F and 108°F) and declines at temperature extremes [17].
In the Texas summer climate, a highly reflective white TPO roof (albedo ~0.75) maintains a surface temperature of approximately
130°F during peak solar irradiance. Assuming an interior data center setpoint of 72°F, the mean temperature of the polyiso board
is approximately 101°F. At this temperature, polyiso performs near its optimal rated value of R-5.6 to R-5.7 per inch.
However, when the membrane degrades and darkens (albedo ~0.40), the surface temperature can exceed 165°F, driving the mean
board temperature up to 118°F. At this elevated temperature, the blowing agents within the closed-cell foam begin to condense,
 increasing thermal conductivity. The effective R-value drops to approximately R-4.9 per inch—a 14% reduction in thermal
resistance exactly when insulation is needed most.
Furthermore, severely degraded roofs often exhibit ponding water and membrane failures that allow moisture ingress. Wet
polyiso insulation suffers catastrophic thermal degradation, losing up to 40–60% of its R-value when saturated [18]. Using the
Moisture Stress Index (MSI) derived from Sentinel-2 shortwave infrared bands, this study identified 87 facilities exhibiting
significant moisture stress.
To quantify this compounding effect, we modeled the dynamic R-value of the insulation layer for all 194 calibrated facilities,
estimating baseline insulation thickness based on the facility build year and the corresponding ASHRAE 90.1 prescriptive
requirements for Climate Zones 2A and 3A (ranging from R-15 continuous insulation pre-2004 to R-25 post-2013) [19].
The results reveal a nuanced reality: because the Texas climate keeps the mean board temperature in the optimal performance
band for much of the year, the purely conductive penalty of temperature derating is negligible across the fleet (and even slightly
negative in some shoulder seasons). However, the moisture penalty is substantial. For the facilities exhibiting high MSI scores, the
estimated loss of thermal resistance due to moisture ingress adds an additional $55,693 in annual cooling energy costs for the
2024 measured cohort. This demonstrates that while temperature derating of polyiso is a factor at extreme peak conditions, the
primary secondary failure mode of a degraded roof is moisture intrusion.

4. The Financial and Environmental Toll
4.1. The Energy Cost Penalty: Quantifying the Invisible Tax
The core financial finding of this study is that the degradation of cool roofs across the Texas data center fleet generates an
estimated $11,257,000 in excess annual cooling energy costs based on 2024 data from 191 measured facilities, with a square-
footage-weighted extrapolation to the full 425-facility Texas portfolio yielding an estimated $20.6 million annually. This figure

The distribution of this penalty is highly skewed. The median facility incurs approximately $28,265 in excess annual costs, but the

specific facility, its verified roof area, and its local solar irradiance data.
At an average Texas commercial electricity rate of $0.065/kWh [6], the $11.26 million annual penalty equates to approximately

The financial penalty is also not uniformly distributed across the state. Facilities in the Houston coastal zone (ASHRAE Zone 2A)

4.2. The Hidden Water Waste: The Cooling Tower Connection
While the energy penalty of degraded roofs is substantial, the corresponding impact on water consumption is arguably more
critical in the context of Texas’s hydrology. Data centers are highly water-intensive, utilizing evaporative cooling towers to reject

Our analysis quantifies the specific water waste attributable solely to roof degradation—the incremental water consumption

atmosphere. More heat to reject means more water evaporated. The degradation of a data center’s roof therefore has a direct,
linear relationship with its cooling tower water consumption.

5. Systemic Risk: The ERCOT Grid Impact
5.1. The Coincident Peak Demand Problem
The localized inefficiencies of individual data centers compound into a systemic vulnerability for the Texas power grid. The ERCOT
grid is uniquely sensitive to summer peak demand, driven primarily by residential and commercial air conditioning loads that
peak on hot summer afternoons. Data centers are traditionally viewed as “flat load” consumers—their power draw is relatively
constant regardless of time of day or season. However, this characterization is inaccurate for data centers with degraded roofs.
When a data center’s roof is degraded, its cooling load increases in direct proportion to solar irradiance. Solar irradiance peaks at
approximately 2:00 PM local time, and the resulting heat gain reaches the cooling system with a thermal lag of approximately two
hours, meaning that the incremental cooling load from roof degradation peaks at approximately 4:00 PM—precisely the period of
highest ERCOT grid stress. This synchronization between degraded-roof cooling load and grid peak demand transforms what
appears to be a private facility management issue into a public grid reliability concern.
5.2. ERCOT Scarcity Events and the Cost of Marginal Demand
We estimate that the degraded roofs across the 191 measured facilities with complete peak-year spectral data add approximately
25.9 MW of coincident peak demand to the ERCOT grid during summer afternoons—extrapolating to an estimated 47.4 MW
across the full 425-facility Texas portfolio. This figure applies a coincidence factor of 0.24 to the theoretical instantaneous peak
heat gain, accounting for thermal lag through the roof assembly (~2 hours), building thermal mass buffering, and the statistical
diversity of peak timing across geographically distributed facilities. While 25.9–47.4 MW may appear modest relative to ERCOT’s
80,000+ MW summer peaks, grid cost is determined at the margin.
ERCOT operates on a marginal pricing model, where the cost of electricity is set by the most expensive generation unit required to
meet demand at any given moment. During peak summer hours, incremental demand forces the dispatch of high-cost peaker
plants, driving wholesale prices toward the $5,000/MWh scarcity cap. Because the albedo penalty is perfectly coincident with peak

 6. Discussion
6.1. The “Build and Forget” Paradigm
The data clearly demonstrates that the current industry paradigm of “build and forget” regarding passive cooling infrastructure is
failing. Developers invest heavily in high-albedo membranes during construction to meet LEED standards, ENERGY STAR
requirements, or local building codes, but the performance of these investments is not tracked after commissioning. As the NAIOP
Research Foundation noted in its January 2026 report, developers are highly focused on “managing near-term and long-term
sustainability risk” during the development phase [9], but this focus rarely extends to ongoing operational verification of passive
systems.
This is partly a structural problem. In many colocation data center models, the tenant pays the utility bills while the landlord or
operator owns the building envelope. This creates a classic “split-incentive” problem [5]: the operator bears the cost of roof
maintenance but does not directly benefit from the energy savings, which accrue to the tenant. The result is systematic
underinvestment in roof maintenance, even when the ROI is highly favorable.
6.2. The ROI of Restoration
For the average Texas data center in this cohort, restoring the roof to its design albedo would yield approximately $58,937 in
annual energy savings and eliminate 145,000 gallons of water waste. The cost of professional cool roof cleaning (the most
common restoration method) ranges from $0.05 to $0.15 per square foot, depending on the facility size and soiling level. For a
facility with 50,000 square feet of roof area (approximately average for this cohort), cleaning would cost $2,500–$7,500 and would
typically need to be repeated every 2–3 years.
The resulting ROI is exceptional: a $5,000 cleaning investment that yields $58,937 in annual energy savings represents an ROI of
over 1,000%. Even for facilities where the energy savings are more modest, the payback period for roof cleaning is typically
measured in weeks to months, not years.
For facilities in the Critical risk tier, where membrane degradation has progressed beyond the point where cleaning is effective, a
full membrane replacement may be warranted. At $3–$8 per square foot installed, a 50,000 SF membrane replacement costs
$150,000–$400,000. With annual energy savings of $100,000–$200,000 for a Critical-tier facility, the payback period is typically 1–3
years—still an excellent return for a capital investment that also extends the life of the roof assembly and reduces the risk of
moisture infiltration.
The 62 facilities flagged for “rapid degradation” in the anomaly detection pipeline represent a particularly urgent subset. These
facilities are experiencing accelerated albedo loss that, if not arrested, will move them from High to Critical risk within 1–2 years,
dramatically increasing both the energy penalty and the cost of eventual remediation.
6.3. Implications for Regulatory Frameworks
The findings of this study have direct implications for the regulatory frameworks governing data center resource consumption in
Texas and beyond. Current regulations focus almost exclusively on the design efficiency of new facilities (e.g., design PUE, WUE,
and LEED certification), with no mechanism for monitoring or enforcing ongoing operational performance.
The PUCT’s announced water use survey [10] is a step in the right direction, but it is unlikely to capture the specific contribution of
passive infrastructure degradation to water consumption. We recommend that future regulatory frameworks consider the
following measures.
Mandatory spectral monitoring would require data centers above a certain capacity threshold to conduct annual or biennial
satellite-based spectral assessments of their roof assemblies, with results reported to the PUCT and TWDB. The technology to do
this at scale is now mature and cost-effective, as demonstrated by this study.
Performance-based permitting would tie water use permits to demonstrated operational performance metrics, including roof
albedo, rather than solely to design specifications. A facility that was permitted based on a specific water footprint should be
required to demonstrate that its passive infrastructure continues to perform at the level assumed in the permit.
Maintenance escrow requirements would require developers to establish maintenance escrow accounts at the time of
permitting, funded at a level sufficient to cover periodic roof cleaning and eventual membrane replacement. This would address
the split-incentive problem by ensuring that funds are available for maintenance regardless of changes in ownership or tenancy.
 Tenant-landlord alignment through model lease provisions could align the incentives of colocation operators and tenants
regarding building envelope maintenance, potentially through shared savings mechanisms where the operator and tenant split
the energy savings generated by roof restoration.
6.4. Limitations and Future Research
This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the Sentinel-2 satellite provides 10-meter to 20-meter
spatial resolution depending on the spectral band, which means that for smaller facilities (roof area < 1,000 m²), the pixel count
within the roof polygon may be insufficient for reliable spectral statistics, particularly for the 20-meter SWIR bands. We applied a
minimum scene count threshold of three valid scene-days per year to mitigate this, but small facilities may still have higher
measurement uncertainty.
Second, the energy impact model uses a fixed COP of 3.5 for all facilities, which does not account for the wide variation in cooling
system efficiency across the cohort. Facilities with older, less efficient cooling systems will incur higher energy penalties per unit
of excess heat gain than those with modern high-efficiency systems.
Third, the study covers only the summer season (June–August), which captures the period of peak solar irradiance and maximum
thermal penalty. A full-year analysis would capture additional energy impacts in spring and fall, though these are expected to be
smaller in magnitude.
Future research should explore the correlation between spectral degradation indices (particularly MSI and BURI) and the physical
condition of the membrane as assessed by infrared thermography or nuclear isotope moisture scanning. Establishing validated
correlations between remote sensing indicators and physical membrane condition would enable more precise prioritization of
maintenance interventions and would strengthen the evidentiary basis for regulatory frameworks.

6.5 Beyond the Roof: The Full Envelope Perspective
The findings of this study underscore the necessity of viewing the data center roof not merely as a weatherproofing layer, but as
an active component of the facility’s thermal management system. The full-envelope model, which incorporates both the primary
solar albedo penalty ($11.26 million annually for the 191 measured facilities) and the secondary moisture degradation penalty
($55,693 annually), confirms that solar reflectance loss is the dominant mechanism—and that the total “invisible tax” of roof
degradation reaches an estimated $20.6 million per year when extrapolated across the full 425-facility Texas portfolio.
However, the roof is only one component of the building envelope. Preliminary modeling conducted alongside this study suggests
that degradation of other passive systems also imposes material energy penalties. Specifically, the degradation of exterior wall
coatings and the failure of window glazing seals (leading to loss of insulating gas fill) are estimated to add an additional $5.3
million and $311,000 in annual cooling energy costs, respectively, across the Texas fleet. When combined with the roof penalty,
the total “invisible tax” of passive envelope degradation approaches $24 million annually.
This full envelope perspective challenges the industry’s singular focus on active cooling efficiency (e.g., PUE optimization through
liquid cooling). While active systems are critical, their efficiency is fundamentally bounded by the thermal load they must reject. A
degraded envelope artificially inflates this load, forcing high-efficiency chillers to work harder to remove heat that should never
have entered the building.
As ASHRAE 90.4 (Energy Standard for Data Centers) continues to evolve, it currently defers envelope requirements to ASHRAE 90.1.
However, the unique operational profile of data centers—continuous high-density internal heat loads combined with mission-
critical reliability requirements—suggests that the industry may need specialized envelope maintenance standards. The empirical
evidence presented here demonstrates that “build and forget” is not a viable strategy for data center envelopes. Continuous
spectral monitoring and proactive restoration are essential to maintaining the design intent of the full building envelope. The
authors are currently seeking industry partners to expand this empirical analysis to include wall and window degradation in
future research.

8. Methodological Robustness: Addressing Common Technical Questions
This section anticipates the technical questions most likely to arise from peer reviewers, facility operators, and policymakers
reviewing these findings. The purpose is not to hedge the conclusions of this study, but to demonstrate that the identified gaps
 are either bounded, non-material, or conservative in direction—meaning the true magnitude of the “invisible tax” is at least as
large as reported, and likely larger.

Q1: Sentinel-2 has a 10-meter spatial resolution. Can it accurately measure individual building roofs?
Short answer: Yes, for the buildings in this study, and the geometry is verified.
At 10-meter resolution, a single Sentinel-2 pixel represents 100 square meters (approximately 1,076 square feet). The median data
center roof in this study covers 29,679 square feet, yielding approximately 28 pure roof pixels per facility. The average roof is
67,110 square feet, yielding approximately 62 pixels. The Statistical API aggregates these pixels using exact GeoJSON polygon
masks, not bounding boxes, eliminating contamination from parking lots, vegetation, or adjacent structures. The mean and
standard deviation of reflectance across all valid pixels within the polygon are returned, providing a statistically robust estimate of
the roof’s spectral state.
For the 44% of facilities with smaller roofs (under 20,000 sq ft), the pixel count drops to approximately 18 pixels. At this scale, edge
effects and mixed pixels become a concern. These facilities are flagged in the database with a small_roof_flag and are excluded
from the per-facility precision claims, though they are included in fleet totals where the averaging effect mitigates individual
errors.
Critically, the polygon quality calibration exercise documented in Section 2.1 manually verified the alignment of all 425 roof
polygons against current satellite imagery, confirming that the spectral extraction is geometrically accurate for the facilities
driving the majority of the reported penalty.

Q2: Atmospheric correction and cloud masking introduce uncertainty. How reliable are the albedo
values?
Short answer: The uncertainty is quantified, bounded, and does not change the conclusions.
Sentinel-2 Level-2A products apply the Sen2Cor atmospheric correction algorithm, which has a stated absolute radiometric
uncertainty of ±0.02–0.05 reflectance units under typical conditions [8]. This uncertainty is applied consistently across all
facilities and all years, meaning it does not introduce differential bias between facilities or across time.
The temporal aggregation strategy—averaging 14–25 valid scene-days per facility-year after strict cloud masking using the Scene
Classification Layer (SCL)—reduces the effective uncertainty of the annual mean to well below the single-scene level. A Monte
Carlo sensitivity analysis (Appendix B) demonstrates that even with ±0.05 reflectance uncertainty applied to every scene, the
fleet-wide albedo trend and the identification of Critical-tier facilities are statistically robust at the 95% confidence level.
Furthermore, the energy penalty model uses the difference between measured albedo and the CRRC baseline (0.55), not the
absolute albedo value. A systematic bias of ±0.03 in absolute albedo translates to a ±5.5% change in the reported penalty—well
within the bounds of the sensitivity analysis.

Q3: The energy penalty model uses a simplified linear heat transfer equation. Real data center cooling is
more complex.
Short answer: The simplification is conservative and well-validated for this application.
The energy penalty model (Section 2.4) calculates the additional cooling load from albedo degradation using the fundamental
heat transfer equation: ΔQ = (α_baseline − α_current) × G_solar × A_roof × (1 − ε_LW), where G_solar is the measured annual
solar irradiance from Google Solar API data and ε_LW is the longwave emittance correction factor. This is the same approach used
by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) in its Cool Roof Calculator and by ASHRAE 90.1 compliance pathways.
The simplification omits second-order effects including: (1) the interaction between roof surface temperature and HVAC intake air
temperature for RTU-dominant facilities; (2) the non-linear relationship between cooling load and chiller COP at part-load
conditions; and (3) the thermal mass buffering effect of the roof assembly. All three of these effects would increase the calculated
penalty relative to the linear model. The reported figures are therefore conservative lower bounds.

Q5: The polygon quality calibration shows many facilities have oversized or contaminated polygons.
Doesn’t this invalidate the spectral data?
Short answer: No. The contamination effects are bounded and the direction of bias is known.
The polygon quality calibration exercise (Section 2.1) classified 194 of 425 facilities as having confirmed, high-quality polygon-to-
building alignment. The remaining facilities fall into categories including POLYGON_OVERSIZED (polygon extends slightly beyond
the building footprint), MULTI_BUILDING_CONTAMINATION (polygon captures a mix of buildings), and BAD_GEOCODE (polygon is
on the wrong parcel entirely).
For POLYGON_OVERSIZED cases, the contaminating pixels are typically parking lots (dark asphalt, albedo ~0.10) or adjacent roofs.
Dark contamination lowers the measured albedo, making the facility appear worse than it actually is. This means the reported
penalty for these facilities is an overestimate, not an underestimate. The fleet-level effect is conservative.
For BAD_GEOCODE cases, the spectral data is unreliable and these facilities are excluded from per-facility precision claims.
However, they represent only 18% of the portfolio by count and a smaller fraction by roof area, and their exclusion does not
materially affect the fleet-level statistics.
All 425 facilities have been polygon-quality calibrated, representing 27.0 million square feet of verified roof area. The 191 facilities
with complete 2024 spectral data represent 16.7 million square feet (61.8% of total portfolio area) and drive the reported energy
penalty. The conclusions of this study rest on this verified subset.

Q6: Rooftop mechanical equipment (RTUs, cooling towers, HVAC units) has different spectral properties
than the membrane. Doesn’t this contaminate the albedo reading?
Short answer: Yes, and the model explicitly corrects for it.
Section 3.7 documents the spectral unmixing methodology developed to address rooftop mechanical contamination. Using the
Building Utilization and Rooftop Infrastructure (BURI) index—derived from Sentinel-2 SWIR bands—the model estimates the
fractional coverage of rooftop mechanical equipment for each facility. The albedo reading is then corrected using a two-
endmember linear mixing model: one endmember for the membrane spectral signature and one for the mechanical equipment
signature.
The correction is validated against the 1210 Integrity Drive case study, where ground-truth mechanical coverage data (25.4% of
roof area) was available from field inspection. The corrected albedo of 0.695 matches the expected performance of a recently
installed TPO membrane, while the uncorrected reading of 0.582 would have incorrectly classified the facility as High-risk. The
correction prevents the artificial penalization of facilities with high rooftop equipment density—a common characteristic of RTU-
dominant data centers in the Richardson Telecom Corridor.

Q7: The study covers only Texas. Are the findings generalizable?
Short answer: Texas is the hardest case, which makes the findings a lower bound for national impact.
 Texas represents the most thermally demanding environment for data center roofs in the continental United States: the highest
solar irradiance, the longest cooling season, and the most extreme peak demand events. If cool roof degradation imposes an
$11.3M annual penalty on the measured Texas cohort under these conditions, the per-square-foot penalty in more temperate
markets (Virginia, Oregon, Ohio) would be lower. However, the relative degradation rates—the rate at which membranes lose
reflectance—are consistent across climates, as documented by Bonanni et al. (2025) [3].
The methodology developed in this study is directly transferable to any geography with Sentinel-2 coverage (global) and a data
center density sufficient to justify fleet-scale analysis. The authors are currently extending the analysis to the Virginia data center
corridor (Northern Virginia / Ashburn), which hosts the world’s largest concentration of data center capacity.

Q8: The study identifies the problem but doesn’t prove that cleaning or replacing the roof actually
restores the measured albedo.
Short answer: The restoration effect is documented in the longitudinal data.
The nine-year time series captures multiple instances of albedo recovery events—step-change increases in measured reflectance
that correspond to documented roof maintenance activities. The 11830 Webb Chapel Road case study (Section 3.5) provides the
most detailed example: the facility’s albedo increased from 0.31 to 0.58 following a documented roof coating application in 2023,
before declining again to 0.39 by 2025 as the coating failed. This real-world trajectory confirms both the efficacy of restoration and
the importance of durable membrane selection over temporary coatings.
The ROI calculations in Section 6.2 are based on the measured pre- and post-restoration albedo values from these documented
events, not on theoretical assumptions. The restoration effect is empirically grounded in the same dataset that identifies the
degradation.

9. Conclusion
Data centers are the engines of the modern digital economy, but their physical footprint imposes very real demands on the analog
world of electricity grids, water supplies, and the atmosphere. This study provides the first empirical, fleet-scale evidence that the
degradation of cool roof membranes across the Texas data center fleet is a widespread, systemic issue with quantifiable financial
and environmental consequences.
By allowing their roofs to darken, data center operators are paying an “invisible tax” of
11.26millionannuallyinexcessenergycostsf orthe191measuredf acilities—extrapolatingtoanestimated20.6 million fleet-wide
across all 425 Texas data centers—and wasting over 25.1 million gallons of water (46.0 million gallons fleet-wide), all while adding
25.9 MW of avoidable coincident peak demand to an already-stressed ERCOT grid (47.4 MW fleet-wide). These costs are not
inherent to the technology of data centers; they are the direct consequence of deferred maintenance on a passive building system
that was designed to provide decades of thermal benefit.
The analysis reveals stark disparities across operators, with some demonstrating exemplary performance and others showing
systemic underinvestment in roof maintenance. The financial case for restoration is overwhelming: for most facilities in this
cohort, the ROI on roof cleaning exceeds 1,000%, with payback periods measured in weeks. For Critical-tier facilities requiring full
membrane replacement, the payback period is typically 1–3 years.
As the AI boom accelerates data center development in Texas and globally, the industry must expand its definition of efficiency
beyond active cooling systems and IT equipment. Advanced liquid cooling and efficient silicon are vital, but they must be built
upon a foundation of optimized, actively managed passive infrastructure. Continuous spectral monitoring—enabled by freely
available satellite data and the analytical frameworks demonstrated in this study—and proactive roof restoration are no longer
just facility maintenance tasks. They are essential strategies for grid resilience, water conservation, and sustainable digital growth
in a state that can afford neither the energy waste nor the water loss.

2.1. Facility Identification and Bounding

The study analyzed 425 data center facilities located within the state of Texas. Facility locations and roof polygons were sourced

[ongitudina[ analysis, and 191 had complete data for the 2024 focal year.

2.2. Remote Sensing and Spectral Extraction

A[bedo (solar reflectance) and related spectral indices were extracted using Sentine[-2 Level-2A (L2A) imagery via the Sentine[ Hub

comparison.

parking lots, vegetation, or adjacent structures.

Sentine[-2 provides multispedra[ imagery at varying spatial resolutions: 10 meters for visible and near-infrared bands (B04, B08)
and 20 meters for shortwave infrared bands (B11). At 10-meter resolution, each pixel represents 100 square meters, yielding

3.8 The Compounding Effect: Insulation Thermal Derating and Moisture Degradation

While the primary mechanism of excess cooling load is the increased surface temperature of degraded membranes, this effect is
compounded by the temperature-dependent performance of the underlying insulation. Modern data center roofs are typically
insulated with po[yisocyanurate (po[yiso) rigid foam board, which provides high thermal resistance per inch. However, the R-value
of polyiso is not static; it is highly dependent on the mean temperature of the board.

Based on testing by the Building Science Corporation (BSC) and the National Roofing Contractors Association (NRC:A), the thermal
resistance of po[yiso peaks at moderate mean temperatures (between 36°F and 108°F) and declines attemperature extremes [17].
In the Texas summer climate, a highly reflective white TPO roof (a[bedo -0.75) maintains a surface temperature of approximately
130°F during peak solar irradiance. Assuming an interior data center setpoint of 72°F, the mean temperature of the polyiso board
is approximately 101°R Atthis temperature, po[yiso performs near its optimal rated value of R-5.6 to R-5.7 per inch.

However, when the membrane degrades and darkens (a[bedo -0.40),the surface temperature can exceed 165°F, driving the mean
board temperature up to 118°F. At this elevated temperature, the blowing agents within the closed-ce[[ foam begin to condense,
 increasing thermal conductivity. The effective R-value drops to approximately R-4.9 per inch-a 14% reduction in thermal
resistance exactly when insulation is needed most.

Furthermore, severely degraded roofs often exhibit ponding water and membrane failures that allow moisture ingress. Wet
po[yiso insulation suffers catastrophic thermal degradation, losing up to 40-60% of its R-value when saturated [18]. Using the
Moisture Stress Index (MSI) derived from Sentine[-2 shortwave infrared bands, this study identified 87 facilities exhibiting
significant moisture stress.

To quantify this compounding effect, we modeled the dynamic R-value of the insulation layer for a[[ 194 calibrated facilities,
estimating baseline insulation thickness based on the facility build year and the corresponding ASHRAE 90.1 prescriptive
requirements for Climate Zones 2A and 3A (ranging from R-15 continuous insulation pre-2004 to R-25 post-2013) [19].

The results reveal a nuanced reality: because the Texas climate keeps the mean board temperature in the optimal performance
band for much of the year, the purely conductive penalty of temperature derating is negligible across the fleet (and even slightly
negative in some shoulder seasons). However, the moisture penalty is substantial. For the facilities exhibiting high MSI scores, the
estimated loss of thermal resistance due to moisture ingress adds an additional $55,693 in annual cooling energy costs for the
2024 measured cohort. This demonstrates that while temperature derating of polyiso is a factor at extreme peak conditions, the
primary secondary failure mode ofa degraded roof is moisture intrusion.

5. Systemic Risk: The ERCOT Grid Impact

5.1. The Coincident Peak Demand Problem

The localized inefficiencies of individual data centers compound into a systemic vulnerability for the Texas power grid. The ERCOT
grid is uniquely sensitive to summer peak demand, driven primarily by residential and commercial air conditioning loads that
peak on hot summer afternoons. Data centers are traditionally viewed as "flat load" consumers-their power draw is relatively
constant regardless oftime ofday or season. However, this characterization is inaccurate for data centers with degraded roofs.

When a data center's roof is degraded, its cooling load increases in direct proportion to solar irradiance. Solar irradiance peaks at
approximately 2:OO PM [oca[ time, and the resu[ting heat gain reaches the cooling system with a thermal lag of approximately two
hours, meaning that the incremental cooling load from roof degradation peaks at approximately 4:00 PM-precisely the period of
highest ERCOT grid stress. This synchronization between degraded-roof cooling load and grid peak demand transforms what
appears to be a private facility management issue into a public grid reliability concern.

6.1. The "Build and Forget" Paradigm

The data clearly demonstrates that the current industry paradigm of "build and forget" regarding passive cooling infrastructure is
fai[ing. Developers invest heavily in high-a[bedo membranes during construction to meet LEED standards, ENERGY STAR
requirements, or local building codes, butthe performance of these investments is not tracked after commissioning. As the NAIOP
Research Foundation noted in its January 2026 report, developers are highly focused on "managing near-term and long-term

Mandatory spectral monitoring would require data centers above a certain capacity threshold to conduct annual or biennial
satellite-based spectral assessments of their roof assemblies, with results reported to the PUCT and TWDB. The technology to do

Performance-based permitting would tie water use permits to demonstrated operational performance metrics, including roof
a[bedo, rather than solely to design specifications. A facility that was permitted based on a specific water footprint should be
required to demonstrate that its passive infrastructure continues to perform atthe level assumed in the permit.

Maintenance escrow requirements would require developers to establish maintenance escrow accounts at the time of
permitting, funded at a level sufficient to cover periodic roof cleaning and eventual membrane replacement. This would address
the split-incentive problem by ensuringthat funds are available for maintenance regardless of changes in ownership ortenancy.

regarding building envelope maintenance, potentially through shared savings mechanisms where the operator and tenant split

6.4. Limitations and Future Research

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the Sentine[-2 satellite provides 10-meter to 20-meter

minimum scene count threshold of three valid scene-days per year to mitigate this, but small facilities may still have higher

Second, the energy impact model uses a fixed COP of 3.5 for a[[ facilities, which does not account for the wide variation in cooling
system efficiency across the cohort. Facilities with older, less efficient cooling systems wi[[ incur higher energy penalties per unit
of excess heat gain than those with modern high-efficiency systems.

Third, the study covers only the summer season (June-August),which captures the period of peak solar irradiance and maximum
thermal penalty. A fu[[-year analysis would capture additional energy impacts in spring and fa[[, though these are expected to be
smaller in magnitude.

Future research should explore the correlation between spectral degradation indices (particularly MSI and BURI) and the physical
